issues.legal_issue: A conviction based on membership in an unlawful assembly cannot stand when the charge and evidence identify only five alleged members, two are acquitted, and the evidence does not establish other members.
material_facts: The charge alleged that five named persons formed the unlawful assembly, and the prosecution evidence was confined to those five.
Two of the five named accused were acquitted, leaving three persons proved to have participated.
The case proceeded on the basis that there was no evidence of additional, unnamed members of the assembly.
issues.conclusion: The remaining accused could not be convicted on the basis of constructive liability for an unlawful assembly, because the proved assembly had fewer than five members.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 141 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code, an unlawful assembly must consist of at least five persons, and section 149 imposes constructive liability on its members for qualifying offences. Five persons need not always be convicted: liability may remain where evidence establishes that unidentified persons were also members. But where the charge and evidence are confined to named persons and acquittals leave fewer than five, section 149 is inapplicable. The Court relied on Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, Bharwad Mepa Dana v. State of Bombay, and Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, explaining that Kartar Singh does not impose an absolute bar on finding that unnamed persons were members.

issues.legal_issue: A participant is constructively liable for a fatal act committed by another when the participants act pursuant to a shared prearranged plan and the fatal act advances their common intention.
material_facts: The appellants shared the motive of the person who delivered the fatal blow.
The appellants and that person concealed themselves behind trees while armed, after learning that the victim would pass that way.
They rushed at and chased the victims, surrounded them, and the appellants participated in the assault while the other participant delivered the fatal blow.
The participants fled together after an alarm was raised.
issues.conclusion: Although the unlawful-assembly basis of the murder conviction could not stand, the appellants were guilty of murder on the basis of their common intention with the person who delivered the fatal blow; the conviction was altered accordingly.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code provides constructive liability where a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention. Common intention requires action in concert, a prearranged plan and prior meeting of minds, and participation in the action; it is distinct from merely having the same or similar intention. The inference of common intention must be necessary from the circumstances. The Court relied on Mahabub Shah v. King Emperor.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for rioting cannot stand when the proved participants in the alleged unlawful assembly number fewer than five.
material_facts: The rioting charge alleged that the five named accused formed the assembly.
Two of those named accused were acquitted, and the evidence did not establish additional, unnamed members.
The remaining proved participants therefore numbered fewer than five.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for rioting was set aside and the appellants were acquitted of that offence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 141 of the Indian Penal Code requires an unlawful assembly to consist of five or more persons. A conviction for rioting, which depends on participation in an unlawful assembly, cannot stand if the proved assembly has fewer than five members. The Court's analysis of the statutory minimum relied on the principles discussed in Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, Bharwad Mepa Dana v. State of Bombay, and Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab.
